# Angular minima reduce to a symmetric block of proper interval cuts

Let C be a convex body in `R x R`. Assume its nonempty integer fibers
are finitely many positive-length intervals and its actual mixed
centroid has an integer base coordinate. Translate that coordinate
and the continuous centroid to zero. Write the fibers as

    K_i=[l_i,r_i],  i in P={-L,...,R},
    w_i=r_i-l_i>0,  M=sum_i w_i,
    sum_i i w_i=0,  sum_i w_i(l_i+r_i)=0.                 (1)

For P={0}, (1) gives `l_0=-M/2,r_0=M/2`. The two nonvertical
half-interval caps attain depth 1/2, while any containing vertical
halfspace contains the entire fiber. This is the first alternative
below. In the other case, positivity and (1) force L,R>=1.

There is a closed ambient halfspace through the centroid that attains
its minimum mixed cap mass. It can be chosen nonvertical and, after
possibly reflecting the continuous coordinate, has margin

    x+a i>=0                                             (2)

for a finite real a. Moreover one of the following alternatives holds:

* The minimizing cap wholly captures no fiber.
* A minimizing cap can be chosen with no integer fiber cut exactly at
  either endpoint, and its properly cut fibers are precisely
  `i=-m,...,m` for some integer `m>=0`. Each nonempty tail outside this
  block is homogeneous: every fiber in that tail is wholly captured,
  or every fiber in that tail is wholly excluded. At least one tail
  is wholly captured in this alternative.

This is an all-fiber-count geometric reduction. It does not estimate
the mass of the captured tails and therefore is not yet a centroid
depth theorem for arbitrary fiber counts.

## 1. Interior of the actual convex hull and line endpoints

Replace C by `C_*=conv(S)`; this preserves S exactly. With at least
two distinct positive interval fibers, C_* is full dimensional. The
actual mixed centroid `(0,0)` lies in its interior. Otherwise a
nonzero supporting affine function, nonnegative on C_* and zero at
the centroid, would have integral zero. It would vanish almost
everywhere on every positive interval fiber. Its continuous
coefficient must consequently be zero; its remaining affine function
of the base would vanish at all indices in P, including two distinct
ones. That would make the supporting function identically zero, a
contradiction.

In particular `l_0<0<r_0`. Any line `x=-a z` through the centroid
meets C_* in a nondegenerate compact segment. Except for its two
endpoints, every point of that segment is in the interior of C_*.
For example such a point is a strict convex combination of the
interior centroid and a more distant point of the segment, so it
has a small Euclidean neighborhood in C_*.

Therefore at most two integer fibers can be cut at an endpoint of
their continuous interval. Such a point must be an endpoint of the
line section. The proper cuts form one consecutive block containing
index zero. A section endpoint at an extreme projection index can
instead lie in the interior of that vertical interval; that fiber
is a proper cut and contributes normally. It is not an endpoint
coincidence of the kind considered below.

Outside the proper block and its possible coincident endpoint fibers,
each side has one consistent type, captured or excluded. If two
fibers on the same side had different types, convexity would force
an additional intersection of the line with C_* between them, in
conflict with its single section interval. Equivalently, the upper
endpoints are concave, the lower endpoints convex, and the proper
section already contains zero.

## 2. The minimum is attained at a finite nonvertical tilt

For the orientation (2), its mass is the continuous piecewise affine
function

    F(a)=sum_i min{w_i,max{0,r_i+a i}}.                  (3)

There are finitely many breakpoints, all among
`a=-r_i/i` and `a=-l_i/i` for nonzero indices. The central interval
is always proper and contributes r_0. For sufficiently large finite
positive a, the mass is constant and equals

    sum_(i>0) w_i+r_0.

For sufficiently negative a it is constant and equals
`sum_(i<0)w_i+r_0`. Thus F attains its global minimum on the real
line; there is no nonattained infimum at an infinite tilt. Apply the
same argument after reflecting x for the other continuous orientation.

The vertical closed cap `z>=0` has mass
`sum_(i>0)w_i+w_0`. It is strictly larger than the displayed finite
positive-tilt plateau because `r_0<w_0`. The vertical cap `z<=0` is
strictly dominated by the negative-tilt plateau for the same reason.
Hence no vertical cap can strictly improve the minimum over finite
nonvertical tilts. In fact both vertical caps are strictly worse than
some finite nonvertical cap through the same point. There is no need
to assume a separate numerical lower bound for vertical caps in this
angular-minimum reduction.

Any containing halfspace can be moved parallel inward until its
boundary passes through the centroid. Its closed translate is a
subset and has no larger mass. These observations prove finite
attainment of the minimum over all ambient containing halfspaces.
Nonvertical boundaries have zero mixed length throughout this step.

## 3. Every one- and two-endpoint cusp

Fix a finite angular local minimum a. Let its properly cut indices
be `-p,...,q`, with p,q>=0, and define

    A=p+1,  B=q+1,  Delta=q-p=B-A,
    S=sum_(i=-p)^q i=Delta(A+B-1)/2.

The only possible coincident fibers are the adjacent indices `-A`
and B, when those belong to P. Call a coincidence U when the line
meets the UPPER endpoint (`r_i+a i=0`, cap mass zero there), and L
when it meets the LOWER endpoint (`l_i+a i=0`, cap mass w_i there).
Write a dash if that side has no coincident fiber.

Each proper fiber contributes derivative i to (3). At a U coincidence
the derivative jumps upward by |i|, while at an L coincidence it
jumps downward by |i|. Computing the two one-sided derivatives gives
the complete table:

| Left type | Right type | F'_-(a) | F'_+(a) | Local-minimum possibilities |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| - | - | S | S | Delta=0 |
| U | - | S-A | S | Delta=0 or 1 |
| L | - | S | S-A | none |
| - | U | S | S+B | Delta=0 or -1 |
| - | L | S+B | S | none |
| U | U | S-A | S+B | Delta=-1,0,1 |
| U | L | S-A+B | S | Delta=0 |
| L | U | S | S-A+B | Delta=0 |
| L | L | S+B | S-A | none |

Here a local minimum requires `F'_-(a)<=0<=F'_+(a)`.
For completeness the integer possibilities in the last column are
exact. If `Delta>=2`, then
`S>=2A+1>A`; if `Delta<=-2`, then `S<=-2B-1<-B`.
The U/U row can therefore only have Delta=-1,0,1. At Delta=1 one
has S=A, and at Delta=-1 one has S=-B. The single-U rows have the
additional required sign of S, yielding their stated subsets. In
either mixed U/L row, S has the same sign as Delta, so the two
derivative signs can coexist only at Delta=0. Any row containing
only downward jumps has its right derivative strictly smaller than
its left derivative, so cannot be a local minimum. This also covers
one-endpoint cusps rather than presuming both endpoints are integral.

## 4. Removing all removable coincidences at the same minimum

Every allowed row except U/U with Delta=0 has a zero one-sided
derivative; for the mixed rows both derivatives are zero. Since
there are only finitely many breakpoints, move a sufficiently small
distance to that flat side. The mass stays exactly the same, all
current coincidences disappear, and no new one appears. At a global
minimum this remains a global minimum.

The proper block after that move is symmetric. Explicitly:

* For U/- with Delta=0, move a upward; its left endpoint stays
  excluded and the existing symmetric block is unchanged. With
  Delta=1, move a downward; the missing negative endpoint enters,
  producing `-p-1,...,p+1`.
* For -/U the reflected choices give the same conclusion.
* For U/U with Delta=1, move a downward: the left endpoint enters
  while the right remains excluded. With Delta=-1, move a upward
  and the right endpoint enters instead. Both new blocks are symmetric.
* For U/L with Delta=0, move a upward: the left endpoint remains
  excluded and the right remains fully captured. The symmetric
  proper block is unchanged. For L/U use the opposite direction.
* With no coincidences, the table already forces Delta=0.

In the exceptional U/U row with Delta=0, the two derivatives are
`-A` and A. This is a strict angular cusp and its proper block is
already symmetric. Both line-section endpoints are upper endpoints
of their fibers; consequently every outer fiber is excluded and
no fiber is wholly captured. This is precisely the first alternative
in the theorem, not an unhandled captured-tail configuration.

If the starting global minimum has any captured fiber, that exceptional
case is impossible. In the mixed rows choose the flat direction above
that retains the captured endpoint as a captured fiber. Other strictly
captured fibers keep their status under sufficiently small perturbations.
The resulting minimum therefore has no coincident integer fibers,
has the symmetric proper block `-m,...,m`, and still has a captured
tail. This proves the claimed second alternative.

## 5. Limits of the reduction

The slope balance is the UNWEIGHTED sum of proper indices, since the
coarea derivative of interval length under the tilt a is i. It must
not be replaced by the volume-weighted base-mean identity (1).
Both identities are available, but they serve different purposes.

The lemma is exact at all breakpoints, includes the finite plateaus
corresponding to infinite angular directions, and retains whole
vertical boundary fibers when comparing vertical caps. It does not
assert that captured tails have small total length, that their upper
endpoint moments can be discarded, or that they can be replaced by
four or five fibers. An additional quantitative inequality is still
needed to bound their contribution for arbitrary fiber counts.
